paras: The attempted lynching of Minnie Pearl took place in Peoria, Illinois, on the night of Sunday, July 5, 1903, when a mob of white people went to the home of Minnie Pearl, a Black woman, intending to kill her. Police had already arrested her, and the mob instead tore down her house and threw her furniture into the river. Wire reports of the averted lynching ran in white papers across the country and were reprinted in two Black weeklies.

According to the Peoria dispatch, Minnie Pearl beat Perry Coombs, an 11-year-old white boy, with a club that afternoon until his body was covered with cuts and welts. The same dispatch gave her reason as the boy having led a mule across her lot. The St. Louis Republic and the Savannah Tribune spelled his name "Combs."

That night a mob that most reports put at 300 white people, and the New-York Tribune at six hundred, set out to kill her. Before it reached her house, police arrested her and took her to the police station. Finding her gone, the crowd tore down the house and threw the furniture into the river. No one was reported injured in the attack on the house.

The dispatch said the local humane society would prosecute her the next morning for the beating. The coverage contains no report of the outcome of that case, and no report that anyone in the mob was arrested.

The story reached the white press as a single wire dispatch, printed on July 6 in the Birmingham Age-Herald under "LYNCHING AVERTED," in the Montgomery Advertiser as "Peoria Mob Wanted to Lynch a Negress," and in the New-York Tribune as "MOB TEARS DOWN HOUSE." Headline writers framed it in different ways: the Saint Paul Globe wrote that "Her Offense Was the Beating of a Boy, but She Is Colored," while the St. Louis Republic called her a "Peoria Amazon" who beat a white boy "unmercifully" and left out the destruction of her house. The Louisville Courier-Journal condensed the story into one sentence of its news summary, noting that the mob, "failing in the attempted lynching," demolished her house.

Other papers kept the item in circulation for several days, with the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier repeating the six-hundred figure, the Owingsville Outlook heading it "PREVENTED A LYNCHING," and digests in Kentucky, Tennessee, Minnesota, Mississippi and South Carolina reprinting it through July 10. Like the white dailies, these reprints treated her beating of the boy as fact.

In the Black press, the Savannah Tribune of July 11 printed the wire text under "SOUGHT TO LYNCH WOMAN" among general news, without comment. Nearly a month later, the Baltimore Afro-American retold the story without names in its "Personal and General" column, describing a mob "robbed of their prey" that wrecked her house. Neither Black paper added detail beyond the wire or wrote an editorial on the case.
Reports differ on the size of the mob, with most copies giving 300 white persons and the New-York Tribune giving six hundred; no source settles the figure.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Minnie Pearl
bases: A mob of white people went to Minnie Pearl's house to kill her and, finding her taken by police, destroyed the house; the papers called it an attempted or averted lynching (A1, A2, A15).
A mob reported at 300 sought her life over her alleged beating of a white boy, but she had been arrested before it arrived and no one was killed (A1, A2, A17); it was an attempted lynching.

Every report, white and Black, traces to one Peoria wire dispatch of July 5 (A1, A6, A8) or a summary of it (A2); no local or independent account was found, though no report contradicts the core events.

accounts.label: Peoria wire report
accounts.gist: A mob of 300 white persons sought the life of Minnie Pearl, who had beaten an 11-year-old white boy with a club because he led a mule across her lot; police took her to the station first, and the mob tore down her house and threw the furniture into the river.

accounts.label: St. Louis Republic version
accounts.gist: A mob of 300 'persons' sought her life; she was arrested before it reached the house, and the humane society would prosecute; the destruction of the house is not mentioned.

accounts.label: Black-press reprints
accounts.gist: The Savannah Tribune ran the wire text in full; the Baltimore Afro-American, a month later, retold it without names and said the mob, 'robbed of their prey', wrecked her house.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the wire under headlines like 'LYNCHING AVERTED' (Age-Herald) and 'MOB TEARS DOWN HOUSE' (New-York Tribune), stating her alleged beating of the boy as fact.
The Saint Paul Globe's subhead, 'Her Offense Was the Beating of a Boy, but She Is Colored', pointed to her race as the reason for the mob.
The St. Louis Republic's 'Peoria Amazon Beat White Boy Unmercifully' put the stress on her alleged attack and left out the mob's destruction of her house.
The Savannah Tribune reprinted the wire under 'SOUGHT TO LYNCH WOMAN' with no comment.
The Baltimore Afro-American's brief, without comment, called the mob's target its 'prey'.

conflicts.note: Same wire text with a different figure; most copies say 300, and no source says which is right.

record_check.dossier: property_damage and pursuit are supported; no siege is reported: the mob reached her house after she had been taken away and destroyed it.
She was arrested and at the police station when the mob came for her at her house; the mob did not attack the station or take her from custody.

The wire ran in at least 12 white papers, July 6-10, 1903; the linked Indianapolis Journal item does not carry it.

info: Sunday, July 5, 1903: the boy was beaten in the afternoon and the mob gathered that night (one version says 'to-day').
Minnie Pearl, described as 'colored' and 'a negress'; she was not harmed, but her house was destroyed.
Accused of beating Perry Coombs (or Combs), a white boy of 11, with a club until he was covered with cuts and welts; the wire said she did so because he led a mule across her lot.
A mob of white people; no one is named.
